questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A promise the course cannot keep
questions.learningObjective: Identify the resource gap that makes a stated promise impossible
questions.stem: A design brief promises every new engineer a personalised dashboard by week six of the training course. Which fact most directly shows the promise cannot be kept?

options.text: Building one dashboard needs 40 engineering hours and only two engineers are available across all six weeks.
The dashboard platform is open source, so no licence cost will be attached to it.
options.misconception: confuses software cost with the engineering time needed

options.text: Week six falls after the pilot group has already finished its project work.
options.misconception: reads a scheduling overlap as a promise failure

options.text: New engineers were told to expect a dashboard in the onboarding email.
options.misconception: treats a prior announcement as proof of delivery

questions.explanation: The promise fails on capacity: forty hours of work against two available engineers. Licence cost and the earlier announcement are true but neither creates engineering hours.
questions.hint: Compare the work promised against the time available.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a uniform promise produces unequal burdens
questions.stem: Explain why a design brief that promises a mentor to every engineer produces a heavier load on some teams than on others.

answer.exemplar: A promise that is the same for everyone is not the same for everyone, because the resources behind it are unevenly distributed. Engineers on teams with a strong internal mentor pool fill the slot quickly from a colleague, while engineers on small or remote teams must wait for a mentor drawn from outside the group, so the wait falls on the group that had least slack. The promise also lands unevenly in cost: the internal mentors are giving time that the external mentors are not being asked to give.

questions.explanation: Unequal burdens follow from unequal resources behind an identical promise. Internal pools absorb the request cheaply while small teams wait on scarce shared capacity.
questions.hint: Ask who supplies the resource in each group.

questions.topic: An unread reading load and the writing that suffers
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the writing failure caused by an unread reading load

stimulus.body: The brief assigns two readings totalling 140 pages in the first fortnight and asks each engineer to submit a 500 word analysis in week three. Last year's cohort read 30 pages on average and their analyses were thin on anything beyond the first section. The instructors have plenty of writing advice ready for them.

questions.stem: Given this brief, which change would most improve the written analyses?

options.text: Give the cohort an extra week before the analysis is due.
options.misconception: treats extra calendar time as a substitute for less reading

options.text: Replace the 140 pages with a 20 page digest and keep the full readings optional.
Run a two hour session that walks through the sections that appeared in past analyses.
options.misconception: assumes a session covers what 140 pages did not

options.text: Add a third critique task so each engineer reads one analysis from a peer.
options.misconception: adds reading volume and calls it peer review

questions.explanation: The analyses fail because the pages were not read, so cutting the required reading removes the cause. Extra time, a walkthrough session, and more peer reading leave the load in place.
questions.hint: Reduce the load before improving the writing.

questions.topic: Making a norm enforceable

questions.stem: A design brief states that engineers must update the shared decision log within 24 hours of a design change. Which addition makes this norm enforceable?

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: Identify a question whose scope exceeds what one answer can cover
questions.stem: Explain why the design brief question asking how the team should improve its engineering practice is too broad to answer usefully.

answer.exemplar: The question spans practices that run at different times and against different measures, so any single answer has to average them into one recommendation that fits none of them well. A reviewer may need faster feedback, a test team may need stable infrastructure, and an operations group may need clearer ownership, and choosing among those is a decision the question has not asked for. A broad question also hides which trade-off the team is willing to make, so the answer can look reasonable and still be unusable.

questions.explanation: A question this wide mixes practices with different owners, timings, and success measures. It produces a recommendation nobody can act on rather than a decision.
questions.hint: Ask which practice the answer is meant to change.

questions.explanation: The item builds the conclusion about improvement into its own wording, so the response confirms rather than tests. Presence at the change and prior ratings are secondary to that.
questions.hint: Read the stem as a statement, not just a question.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Explain how over-promising concentrates cost on the least protected group
questions.stem: Explain why promising a same day turnaround on every change tends to burden the team that already has the heaviest workload.

answer.exemplar: A same day promise reads as one commitment to everyone, but the turnaround depends on the reviewer queue each team sits behind. The team with the most changes in flight has the deepest queue, so its engineers are the ones who most often wait longer than a day despite the promise being identical on paper. That team also has the least capacity to absorb a slipped release, because it has already committed its people to more work. The promise therefore converts into a regressive tax on the busiest group.

questions.explanation: The promise sounds uniform but the queue depth behind it is not, so the deepest queue produces the most misses. The cost concentrates on the busiest team rather than spreading evenly.
questions.hint: Ask where the longest queue sits.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A norm nobody enforces
questions.learningObjective: Explain why announcing a norm does not create enforcement
questions.stem: Explain why repeatedly announcing a documentation rule at the start of team meetings fails to make engineers document their decisions.

answer.exemplar: Announcement delivers information without delivering a consequence, so it changes what people know and not what pays. If a decision goes undocumented and nothing about the team's work changes, the rational choice is still to skip it, and the announcement simply adds noise to the next meeting. People also stop attending to repeated messages, so even the informational effect decays. Enforcement needs the missed rule to cost something, which an announcement by definition cannot do.

questions.explanation: An announcement supplies information but no consequence, so skipping the rule stays rational and the message decays as it repeats. Enforcement needs a missed rule to change something.
questions.hint: Ask what a missed rule costs the person.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A promise the course cannot keep
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a broken promise from a merely inconvenient one
questions.stem: Explain why the promise that every participant will finish a personal side project during the course is harder to keep than the promise of a shared workshop demo.

answer.exemplar: The two promises differ in how much of the outcome is inside each participant's control. A shared demo is produced by the group and survives one person's slow progress, while a personal project depends on each engineer's own available hours, their own assignment, and their own judgement about when something is good enough. Any of those can absorb the whole window without anyone failing on purpose. The personal promise also multiplies across the cohort, so one schedule conflict per person becomes many individual misses at once.

questions.explanation: A personal outcome depends on each participant's own hours and judgement, so ordinary life absorbs it and one miss per person multiplies. A shared demo is produced collectively and survives delay.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the outcome one person controls.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Preparation that no one can verify
questions.learningObjective: Explain what would make preparation checkable
questions.stem: Explain what would have to be true for a requirement to prepare a design review before the session to be verifiable.

answer.exemplar: Verification needs a link between the preparation and something that only prepared people produce. If the reviewer can ask about a specific decision in the design, a claim of preparation becomes testable, and a failure to answer reveals that the preparation did not happen. A checklist of who confirmed, or a sign-up sheet, records only that someone said yes, which costs nothing and so measures very little. The preparation also needs to be attached to a deadline and a named owner, otherwise there is no moment at which it can be judged.

questions.explanation: Verifiable preparation requires an artifact or a question only a prepared person could produce, tied to a deadline and an owner. Confirmations record statements, not preparation.
questions.hint: Ask what prepared people produce that others cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of asking a question with no success measure
questions.stem: Explain why a brief question about whether the new release process is working well cannot settle a decision.

answer.exemplar: Without a stated measure, working well collapses into an opinion, and opinions on a shared process tend to converge on the polite answer rather than the true one. Two engineers can give opposite verdicts from the same release history, which means the discussion cannot end by evidence. The absence of a measure also removes the test that would come later, so even a decision that improved the process could not be recognised as an improvement. Asking for a named measure would give the group both a way to answer now and a way to check the answer in three months.

questions.explanation: With no measure the question invites a polite opinion rather than evidence, so the group cannot converge, and it also removes the later test that would show whether a decision helped.
questions.hint: Ask what would count as good, and when.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Explain why uniform access still produces unequal service
questions.stem: Explain why a help desk that promises every engineer a response within one hour still gives some engineers a much worse service than others.

answer.exemplar: A one hour promise describes the queue at the front door, and queues are not the whole service. Engineers working across time zones send requests when the desk is closed, so their message waits until the next working period rather than one hour, while the same request sent at nine in the morning is answered inside the promise. Second, the depth of the queue at the moment of arrival differs by team, and a team that spikes requests around a release inherits a longer wait. The promise is uniform on paper and uneven in delivery.

questions.explanation: Time zone arrivals and uneven queue depth make identical promises produce different waits, so the uniformity is only in the wording. The gap between arrivals and desk hours explains it.
questions.hint: Ask when requests arrive relative to the working day.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A norm nobody enforces
questions.learningObjective: Explain why peer pressure alone fails to enforce a norm
questions.stem: Explain why relying on peer approval alone does not make a coding standard enforceable in a large team.

answer.exemplar: Peer approval works only where people want the approval, and that desire runs out when the work is urgent or the reviewer is someone whose opinion nobody values. With no external consequence, the norm survives only as a habit among people already inclined to follow it, and any schedule pressure lets a small group quietly opt out. Once a few exceptions exist and nothing happens, the norm stops being a rule and becomes a preference. A mechanism that still applies when the work is urgent is what closes that gap.

questions.explanation: Peer approval depends on wanting approval and disappears under pressure, so a few exceptions with no consequence turn the norm into a preference. A rule must hold when work is urgent.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when nobody is watching.

questions.explanation: A merge check applies at the moment of pressure. Quarterly reports, guidelines, and reminders all leave the test optional exactly when the schedule is tightest.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a question that hides a trade-off
questions.stem: Explain why the question of standardising the tooling across all teams hides a decision that has to be made explicitly.

answer.exemplar: Standardising looks like a single question but contains several contested choices: how much money to spend, how long the migration takes, whether legacy services must be converted, and whose tooling is treated as the standard. A yes answer commits the team to all of them at once, and a no answer commits them to continuing the divergence, so the brief hides a set of decisions inside a single word. Engineers asked to respond to the general version tend to answer the version that costs their own team least, which is why the choices need to be pulled out and put to the group.

questions.explanation: A yes or no answer on standardising commits the group to cost, timeline, migration, and whose standard applies all at once, so several decisions hide inside one word.
questions.hint: Ask what a yes answer actually commits them to.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a broad question wastes the time it was meant to save
questions.stem: Explain why a broad question in a design brief wastes more time than a narrow one during the review it is meant to support.

answer.exemplar: A broad question forces every participant to interpret the scope before they can answer it, and each participant interprets it differently, so the meeting starts with a debate about the question rather than the subject. The answers that arrive cover different slices of the territory, so the group has to reconcile them before it can do anything, which usually produces a list nobody owns. A narrow question arrives pre-interpreted, so the time goes to the decision itself. The apparent efficiency of asking broadly is an illusion created by skipping the framing step.

questions.explanation: Broad questions spend the meeting on agreeing what is being asked and reconciling unrelated answers, so time goes to framing. Narrow questions arrive pre-interpreted and get to the decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the first ten minutes of the meeting cover.

questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single promised service splits along a fault line
questions.stem: Explain why a promise of a shared documentation wiki can leave one group of engineers unable to find anything useful.

answer.exemplar: A shared wiki promises one source of truth, but the value of it depends on whether anyone's material is in it. Engineers working on an older product line often find the wiki dominated by material from the current one, so searching for their context returns nothing relevant and the promise is technically kept while the service is empty for them. The problem is not access but coverage, and it runs along the line of what the early writers happened to cover. Promising one source of truth without checking coverage lets that split persist.

questions.explanation: A wiki can satisfy the promise of a single source while holding little for a particular product line, so the fault line is coverage rather than access. Nothing checks what early writers included.
questions.hint: Ask what the early writers happened to document.

questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a preparation claim carries any information
questions.stem: Explain why asking engineers to confirm that they read a specification before the review does not verify that they read it.

answer.exemplar: A confirmation is a claim whose cost is one word, so it tells you what someone is willing to say rather than what they did. Nobody loses anything by confirming, and the people least prepared are under no more pressure to confirm than the people who read carefully, so the responses carry almost no information about preparation. It also produces a false record: the meeting minutes will show every participant prepared, which quietly discourages anyone from admitting they could not finish. A verifiable version asks about content that only a reader could supply.

questions.explanation: Confirmations cost nothing, so they record willingness to say yes rather than actual reading, and they produce misleading minutes. Verifying requires asking about content only a reader could supply.
questions.hint: Ask what a confirmation costs the person giving it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question too broad to answer
questions.learningObjective: Turn a broad question into a decision with an owner and a date
questions.stem: Explain how you would turn the broad question about improving engineering practice into two or three answerable questions for a planning day.

answer.exemplar: Start by listing what has actually gone wrong recently rather than what ought to be improved, because recent failures are specific and each one names a practice worth examining. Turn those into questions that each have one owner, one measure, and one deadline, such as which change caused the most rework in the last quarter or where release waits are accumulating. Two or three of those can be debated in three hours, and each can be answered with evidence that already exists. The broad version could be discussed for a day and still produce nothing anyone could start.

questions.explanation: Convert the broad question into recent specific failures, then give each one an owner, a measure, and a deadline. Those can be debated and answered with evidence that already exists.
questions.hint: Start from what went wrong, not from what should improve.

questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism by which a shared promise becomes unequal
questions.stem: Explain how a promise of equal access to a scarce reviewer produces unequal waiting times across teams.

answer.exemplar: Access is equal at the door and unequal in the queue, because the number of engineers competing for the reviewer differs by team. A large team generates several requests in the same week and fills the reviewer's capacity early, while a small team sends one and waits behind the backlog the large team created. The small team then experiences the promise as broken even though it never exceeded its allowance, and the teams that arrived early never learn that the promise is uneven. Equal access to a scarce resource only produces equal service when demand is also equal.

questions.explanation: Equal access does not mean equal service, because team sizes set how much of the scarce reviewer each one consumes. Teams arriving behind a burst wait longer without breaking the promise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A question that supplies its own answer
questions.learningObjective: Identify a question whose wording excludes the answer it should allow
questions.stem: One design brief asks engineers how satisfied they are with the new release tooling that replaced the old scripts. Which feature of the wording most limits what the answers can reveal?

options.text: The question compares two tools, so answers collapse into a preference between them.
options.misconception: treats comparison as the flaw.

options.text: The question names the tooling, so engineers will search their memory for evidence.
options.misconception: assumes recall effort is the main source of bias

options.text: The question asks for satisfaction, which engineers rarely report honestly.
options.misconception: claims a truthfulness problem the wording does not create

options.text: The question uses satisfied, so it cannot capture partial or negative reactions.

questions.explanation: A single satisfaction scale has no room for partial use or specific complaints. Comparison, recall effort, and honesty are separate questions that the wording does not raise.
questions.hint: Ask what a dissatisfied engineer could possibly say.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A promise the course cannot keep
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a promise that fails on timing from one that fails on capacity
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a promise that fails because it took too long and a promise that fails because there was never enough capacity to deliver it.

answer.exemplar: A timing failure means the work was achievable and the schedule around it slipped, so the same output delivered later would have satisfied the promise, and the remedy is usually a better plan. A capacity failure means the work exceeded the people, hours, or tools available, so no schedule fixes it and the only remedies are more resources or a smaller promise. Telling the two apart matters because a timing failure can be addressed by the team while a capacity failure has to go back to whoever set the promise in the first place.

questions.explanation: A timing failure means the work was possible but late, so better sequencing can fix it. A capacity failure means no schedule works, so the promise itself or the resourcing behind it must change.
questions.hint: Ask whether more time alone would have been enough.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an over-promise lands unevenly
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether an uneven promise can be made fair by priority order

stimulus.body: The brief promises a same day review response to every engineer. An engineer on the platform team notes that a colleague on the data team received a response in twenty minutes. The brief gives no ordering rule for who is served first.

questions.stem: Given the brief, which judgement about the difference in service is best supported?

options.text: The difference comes from arrival time and queue order.
The difference proves the platform team is favoured by the review service.
options.misconception: reads one fast response as deliberate favouritism

options.text: The difference shows the promise works as intended for most engineers.
options.misconception: generalises from a single response to the whole cohort

options.text: The difference means the promise should be replaced with a best effort statement.
options.misconception: jumps to a wording fix without diagnosing the mechanism

questions.explanation: With no ordering rule, who is served depends on when requests arrive and on queue order, so a fast response for one engineer says nothing about the rest. Favoured teams skip that mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what decides the order of service.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An unread reading load and the writing that suffers
questions.learningObjective: Produce a reading plan that supports the required writing
questions.stem: Engineers must read a 120 page guide and write a 500 word architecture note. Which reading and writing plan gives the note the best chance of being well argued?

options.text: Read the whole guide in one evening, then write the note while the wording is fresh.
options.misconception: optimises for recall of wording rather than for argument

options.text: Read the guide in three sittings, note the three decisions it forces.
Skim the guide for headings, write the note from the table of contents, then check the guide.
options.misconception: treats structure as a substitute for having read the content

options.text: Assign each engineer a different third of the guide and pool the summaries before writing.
options.misconception: divides the reading so that no one reads enough to argue

questions.explanation: Reading in sittings and extracting the decisions the guide forces gives the note argument to work with. One evening and skimming give notes without a shared basis.
questions.hint: Extract arguments from the text, not just its headings.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Preparation that no one can verify
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a preparation requirement should exist at all
questions.stem: Stage one: the reading brief requires every engineer to read a 150 page report before a workshop that lasts 90 minutes. Stage two: which judgement about the requirement is best supported?

options.text: The requirement is sound and should be enforced with a confirmation from each engineer.
options.misconception: accepts an unverifiable requirement and a weak check

options.text: The requirement should stay because engineers benefit from exposure to long reports.
options.misconception: keeps it for general exposure.

options.text: The requirement is not worth keeping in that form, because nothing in the workshop depends on full reading.
The requirement is sound and the workshop should be lengthened to cover the report.
options.misconception: fixes the format by expanding the meeting.

questions.explanation: A requirement that only asks for exposure nobody relies on should be cut or reshaped. Confirmation, general benefit, and a longer meeting all keep an activity the session does not need.
questions.hint: Ask what the workshop actually does with the report.
